nameStory: This mussel earned its name from its remarkable ability to produce beautiful freshwater pearls, making it highly prized throughout history. The thick, lustrous mother-of-pearl lining inside its shell gave pearl hunters hope of finding treasures within. Its scientific name Margaritifera literally means 'pearl-bearing,' celebrating this legendary gem-making talent.
description: The freshwater pearl mussel is an endangered bivalve mollusk that lives buried in the sandy or gravelly bottoms of clean, cold streams and rivers. These dark-shelled clams can grow quite large and have incredibly thick, iridescent mother-of-pearl coating their inner shells. They're filter feeders that spend their lives slowly sifting nutrients from flowing water. What's most remarkable is their incredible longevity - some individuals can live over 200 years, making them among the longest-lived animals on Earth.

idTips.label: Shell interior
idTips.description: The inside reveals a thick, lustrous mother-of-pearl layer that feels smooth and cool to the touch, with an almost metallic shine that catches light beautifully

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Oval to kidney-shaped shell that feels heavy and solid in your hands, with a slightly curved profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Shell exterior
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish outer shell surface that often feels rough or bumpy, sometimes with greenish tints on younger specimens

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Can grow quite large, with older specimens reaching the size of your palm and feeling surprisingly hefty when picked up

idTips.label: Growth rings
idTips.description: Concentric ridges on the shell exterior that you can feel with your finger, like tree rings telling the story of many decades of slow growth

habitat: These mussels require exceptionally clean, cold, fast-flowing streams and rivers with sandy or gravelly bottoms where they can partially bury themselves. They're found in pristine waterways throughout northern New England, particularly in areas with good water quality and minimal pollution. They need well-oxygenated water and often occur in the same streams where native trout thrive.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot empty shells along streambanks after ice-out and spring floods have shifted stream sediments. Living mussels begin their most active feeding period as water temperatures rise.
seasonality.summer: Living mussels are most active in their filtering, though they remain largely buried with only their feeding siphons visible at the sediment surface. Empty shells may be found along popular swimming holes.
seasonality.fall: Mussels slow their activity as water temperatures drop. This is often when freshly exposed shells are easiest to find along stream edges after summer's low water.
seasonality.winter: Mussels become dormant under ice and snow. Shell hunting is limited, but ice-out can reveal specimens that didn't survive the winter along stream margins.

funFact: Some freshwater pearl mussels alive today were already adults when the American Revolution began - they can live over 250 years, making them potentially the longest-lived animals in New England and older than the oldest known trees in the region!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other freshwater mussels, but the extraordinarily thick, lustrous mother-of-pearl interior is the giveaway - other mussels have much thinner, less brilliant nacre. Remember: if the inside doesn't shine like a mirror, it's not a pearl mussel.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'freshwater pearl mussel,' this species is different from the mussels that produce most commercial pearls today, which come from Asian and other North American species. The pearls from this species were historically so prized that overharvesting contributed to its endangered status - it's now illegal to collect them in most areas.
compareHints: This is the only Margaritifera species in New England, but it differs from other local freshwater mussels in the Unionidae family by its much thicker shell, more brilliant interior nacre, and preference for faster-flowing, colder water. While other mussels prefer slower rivers and ponds, pearl mussels need the constant flow of clean streams and have that unmistakable mirror-like inner shell that other species simply can't match.
